new_value: • Baudhayana Sulva Sutra (composed c. 800–500 BCE) contains the earliest known Indian formulation of the Pythagorean theorem, stating that the area produced by the diagonal of a rectangle equals the sum of the areas produced by its length and breadth (relating lengths of sides of a right-angled triangle). • Why Option B is incorrect: While Sulva Sutras approximated circle squaring, the precise calculation of pi (approximated as 3.1416) is credited to Aryabhata I (499 CE) in the Aryabhatiya, not the Baudhayana theorem. • Why Option C is incorrect: Logarithmic principles were developed in 17th-century Europe by John Napier, though early Indian work on powers/indices appears in Jaina texts like the Anuyogadvara Sutra, not Baudhayana. • Why Option D is incorrect: The normal distribution (Gaussian curve) is an 18th-century development in modern probability formulated by Abraham de Moivre and Carl Friedrich Gauss. • Often confused with: The Pythagorean theorem; Baudhayana stated this geometric principle at least two centuries before Pythagoras, using it to construct Vedic fire altars (vedis).
issues_found: The question refers colloquially to the 'Baudhayana theorem', which is a modern pedagogical name for the geometric rule regarding right-angled triangles found in Baudhayana's Sulva Sutra.
